data.title: COP31: Singapore authorises first carbon project with Rwanda for international emissions offsetting
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore has authorised its first-ever carbon credit project under its bilateral carbon market agreements.

Rwanda is the first among partner countries to have a project approved to generate credits that could be used to offset the city-state’s national emissions, and those of carbon tax-liable companies.

The project is the first to be approved under a legally binding framework, known as an implementation agreement, signed by Singapore and Rwanda in May 2025. The framework governs the generation and transfer of carbon credits between the two countries under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

As required under Article 6, which governs rules on the bilateral and international transfer of carbon credits, Rwanda has also issued authorisation for the project.

This means that credits generated from the project can be used to meet Singapore’s climate targets, and that Rwanda, as the host country, will increase its reported emissions by the amount of carbon credits it has transferred to Singapore.

Known as a corresponding adjustment, this accounting mechanism is a core requirement under Article 6 to avoid double-counting – that is, having the same emissions reduction counted towards both countries’ climate targets.

One carbon credit represents a reduction or removal of one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e).

Developed by Climate Bridge International, the authorised project aims to improve access to safe drinking water for Rwandans, which is one of the country’s climate priorities, the National Environment Agency said on Saturday (Nov 14) at the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit.

By distributing 300,000 ceramic water filters to households and early childhood development centres across Rwanda with a focus on its western province, the project is expected to benefit around 1.8 million people.

The filters will provide households and the centres with access to safe drinking water without the need to boil water using firewood or charcoal.

“By reducing reliance on these fuels for water treatment, the project will also reduce associated emissions and indoor air pollution,” NEA said. “The reduced need to collect firewood is expected to free up time for education, income-generating activities and community participation.”

The project is expected to mitigate around 780,000 tCO2e between 2026 and 2030. An initial 10,000 water filters started being distributed in June, with the remainder to be progressively deployed in 2027.

NEA said that this first authorisation marks a milestone in Singapore’s international carbon market cooperation, and that more than 20 projects are currently undergoing assessment under the implementation agreement between Singapore and Rwanda.

Despite signing 12 implementation agreements – six of which have been operationalised – no project has received the necessary authorisation until now. Such authorisation will pave the way for credits that meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria to be issued and transferred to the city-state.

Singapore has previously set a target of peaking greenhouse gas emissions around 2028, with a reduction to around 60 million tCO2e by 2030.

Besides helping Singapore offset its emissions to meet its interim climate targets, carbon tax-liable companies may also look forward to offsetting 5 per cent of their taxable emissions.

They have not been able to do so due to the lack of supply of such credits, and have therefore been allowed to roll over their unused offsets in 2025 to this year. Companies can only use credits that meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria laid out in the International Carbon Credits framework to offset their emissions.

Separately, Singapore and Bangladesh have inked a preliminary carbon credits deal, also on the sidelines of COP31, which is taking place at Antalya, Turkey. The memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed on Saturday will pave the way for both countries to trade carbon credits aligned with Article 6. Under the MOU, both countries will work towards an implementation agreement that sets out how carbon credits can be transferred from Bangladesh to Singapore in accordance with Article 6. The MOU also enables the exchange of best practices and knowledge for the development of high-integrity carbon markets and the identification of mutually beneficial Article 6-compliant carbon credit projects.

This will support both countries in achieving their climate targets, while promoting sustainable development, said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry. The agreement was signed by Singapore’s Permanent Secretary for Sustainability and the Environment Melvyn Ong and Bangladesh’s State Minister for the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shaikh Faridul Islam.

data.title: PM Wong to attend Asean Summit in Manila, with digital economy, energy security on agenda
data.description:
[MANILA] Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will attend the 49th Asean Summit and related meetings from Sunday (Nov 15) to Tuesday in Manila, where regional leaders will discuss ways to deepen economic integration, strengthen energy security and accelerate the green energy transition.

The meetings will also focus on opportunities in the digital and green economies, as well as efforts to strengthen the region’s resilience against external shocks, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said on Saturday.

Held under the Philippines’ chairmanship theme of “Navigating Our Future, Together”, the summit will see leaders reaffirm their commitment to Asean’s community building efforts and discuss ways to promote an open and inclusive regional architecture.

They will also explore ways to strengthen cooperation with external partners to advance peace, stability and prosperity in the region, PMO said.

Among the key economic developments expected at the summit is the signing of the Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement, after negotiations on the pact concluded in May.

The agreement aims to make it easier for businesses to operate across South-east Asia by simplifying digital trade procedures, facilitating cross-border data flows and strengthening digital payments and electronic transactions.

Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said in May that the pact would help businesses – particularly small and medium-sized enterprises – tap opportunities in the region’s expanding digital economy.

Energy security is also expected to be a key focus of the summit, amid uncertainty in global energy markets and efforts to reduce the region’s reliance on fossil fuels.

Asean energy ministers reached a consensus in October on an enhanced memorandum of understanding for the Asean Power Grid, a regional initiative aimed at strengthening electricity connectivity and facilitating cross-border power trade.

The Manila meetings will also bring together Asean leaders and their counterparts from major partner countries.

PM Wong will meet leaders from Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea and the US, as well as the United Nations, at the related summits.

US President Donald Trump is expected to attend the Asean-US Special Summit on Tuesday, according to the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs. He is also scheduled to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on the sidelines of the meetings.

The meetings come ahead of Singapore’s assumption of the Asean chairmanship in 2027.

Speaking at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore in October, PM Wong said the Republic would seek to accelerate economic integration within Asean and strengthen the grouping’s connections with existing partners.

Singapore would also explore opportunities to deepen ties with other regions, including Latin America, Africa and the Middle East, he said.

In Manila, PM Wong will be accompanied by his wife and Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan.

While PM Wong is away, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong will be the acting prime minister.

data.title: Chinaâs bus giant Yutong wants to win the world over, but some are wary
data.description:
[ZHENGZHOU] Inside a manufacturing complex the size of 200 football fields in the capital of China’s central Henan province, buses wrapped in a kaleidoscope of international liveries roll off assembly lines every few minutes.

These “new energy” vehicles are among the tens of thousands produced annually by Chinese commercial vehicle giant Yutong and shipped to all corners of the globe, including Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and South-east Asia.

In Singapore, 100 of the company’s single-deck electric buses are slated to join the public bus fleet progressively from the end of 2026.

They will add to the 20 Yutong electric public buses already in service and the more than 700 privately registered Yutong coaches and tour buses operating across the island.

Such is Yutong’s reach, especially in the fast-growing electric bus market, with the publicly listed company operating buses in more than 100 countries.

It said it holds more than 10 per cent of the global market, putting it ahead of domestic rivals such as BYD and King Long, as well as European incumbents including Volvo and Daimler Buses.

In 2025, Yutong’s overseas revenue surpassed domestic sales for the first time in the company’s now 63-year history, with orders growing rapidly in countries such as Saudi Arabia, Mexico and Uzbekistan.

Yet, ask company executives and they say the road to becoming an enduring global powerhouse has just begun.

“Our manufacturing and industrial capability – our ‘hard power’ – is good. But our ‘soft power’ is relatively lacking,” Yutong Bus global brand director Jason Huang told The Straits Times at the company’s Zhengzhou headquarters in late October.

Huang noted that automotive stalwarts Toyota and Volkswagen took decades to move beyond their domestic bases and establish long-term sustainable growth abroad.

“We believe customer satisfaction across our products, sales and services is the true foundation of our brand,” he said, adding that Yutong hopes to strengthen its brand reputation and pragmatically deepen its international footprint.

But against a backdrop of rising trade protectionism and heightened national security sensitivities, this expansion has set off alarm bells.

As Yutong works to win over more customers, some buyers are increasingly weighing the commercial benefits against the risks of relying on a foreign supplier for critical infrastructure.

Security issues

In October 2025, Yutong made headlines when Norwegian public transport operator Ruter conducted tests that suggested the manufacturer’s electric city buses could, in theory, be shut down remotely.

Yutong rejected the claim, saying such an intervention is technically impossible.

Ruter, which runs about 300 Yutong buses, also stressed that its findings applied to connected vehicles in general, rather than a single manufacturer or country of origin.

In Singapore, the Land Transport Authority clarified in late 2025 that its existing Yutong fleet does not support over-the-air software updates and cannot be remotely controlled.

Still, anxieties over espionage and data security risks persist.

When asked about this, Yutong cited a September 2026 audit commissioned by Danish transit agency Movia, in which the Chinese manufacturer scored top marks across several benchmarks. These include compliance with United Nations cybersecurity standards and software update management.

The third-party audit by EY assessed electric bus models from seven Chinese and European suppliers, as well as electric passenger cars from Tesla and BYD.

Yutong executives also stressed that telematics data from its vehicles in Europe – stored at a data centre in Germany – cannot be accessed without the customer’s explicit authorisation.

“This approach applies not only in Europe but also in markets such as Singapore, Australia and elsewhere,” Huang said.

Alongside security concerns, the rise of Chinese bus makers has also fuelled anxiety over price competition and the future of legacy manufacturers.

This friction is particularly sharp in Europe, where Chinese brands captured 9 per cent of the total bus market and 28 per cent of the zero-emission segment in 2025, compared with 7 per cent in electric passenger cars, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).

These inroads have shaken local bus makers.

In Britain, coachbuilder Alexander Dennis blamed fierce competition from overseas suppliers when it announced plans in June 2025 to cease manufacturing in Scotland.

Electric bus maker Wrightbus has called on London for more state support to protect home-grown companies.

In October 2026, ACEA called for urgent action to address a widening competitive gap, citing a EU bus trade deficit that grew from €1.6 billion (S$2.3 billion) in 2023 to €2.9 billion in 2025.

The auto industry lobby group also noted that European bus manufacturers are losing ground in Latin America, Africa and Asia, where they once dominated.

In response, some governments have begun to tighten procurement policies.

In August 2026, Norway proposed limiting public bus purchases from countries with which it lacks formal security pacts, including China. It also proposed an exemption to its zero-emissions mandate for buses on national security grounds.

In Denmark, director of traffic operations at Movia, Jeppe Gaard, said in response to ST’s queries that the transport agency is currently considering additional cybersecurity requirements for buses in future tenders, including those concerning remote access and software updates.

He said the Danish National Social Appeals Board, an independent government body, has also confirmed that Movia may legally introduce requirements concerning the origin of electric buses in future tenders, as long as they are within EU regulations.

Meanwhile, new competitors are emerging too.

India, for example, has deployed subsidies to build out a domestic electric bus manufacturing sector that has started exporting to countries such as Mauritius and Tanzania.

Compelling reasons

China-based transport expert Lee Der-Horng, told ST that China’s advantage stems from an integrated industrial ecosystem, not just pricing.

“Attributing China’s current competitiveness entirely to subsidies overlooks the substantial advantages generated by economies of scale, accumulated engineering expertise, supply chain efficiency, and intense domestic competition,” said Lee, who is a fellow at the Academy of Engineering Singapore.

However, Lee noted that the broader issue is not just whether a product is worth buying, but whether long-term dependence on it is acceptable.

“The more equipment depends on a supplier’s software and continuing support, the more buyers need to ask: if that relationship breaks down, can we keep operating? Buses make this especially visible because service disruptions directly affect people’s daily lives.”

For Yutong, dealing with competition and geopolitical headwinds is part and parcel of international expansion, which has become crucial as the company sees a limit to its growth in the domestic Chinese market due to the high-speed rail lines and urban metro networks.

Huang noted that every country has its own import and export policies, including measures to protect domestic manufacturing.

In markets where imports of fully assembled vehicles face stiff restrictions, such as Malaysia, Yutong ships components such as the motor and chassis and works with local partners that do the final assembly.

It maintains more than 10 such local bases worldwide, including in Kazakhstan and Qatar.

The company added that stationing Chinese engineers at these foreign assembly plants ensures the build quality matches that of its Zhengzhou factory, where buses undergo a barrage of tests before shipment.

For transport operators, the commercial case for Chinese buses remains compelling.

In an August 2025 submission to the Copenhagen municipal government, Denmark’s Movia calculated that switching away from Chinese electric buses would cost an extra 13 million Danish kroner (US$1.9 million) to 26 million Danish kroner a year.

It also pointed to delivery delays from European suppliers and superior battery warranties from Chinese manufacturers.

Movia’s Gaard said Chinese-manufactured buses, which account for the majority of the transit agency’s fleet, generally perform very well in daily operations.

“Every operator wants the same thing,” said Colin Anderson, general manager of Tropic Wings, a tour operator in Cairns, Australia, which has operated Yutong buses since 2014.

“You want a bus that will do the job when you want it to… It’s a fairly basic answer, but that’s what the business is,” he told ST. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CDL, Sats, AEM, StarHub, NTT DC Reit, SBS Transit, Centurion
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 12):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier posted net profit of S$209.7 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, up from S$52.4 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to stronger operating profit and a lower share of losses from associate Air India. Revenue rose 14.3 per cent to a record S$5.6 billion, while operating profit rose 16.3 per cent to S$463.7 million from a year earlier. For the first half of FY2026, SIA’s net profit fell 43.9 per cent to S$133.9 million year on year. The board declared an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.02 a share and an interim special dividend of S$0.05 a share, bringing the total payout to S$0.07 a share. Shares of SIA closed 0.4 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$7.17 on Wednesday, before the news.

City Developments Limited (CDL) : The property group said it expects to post a “significantly weaker” financial performance for its second half ending Dec 31. Certain capital-recycling deals that the group had earlier expected to materialise in the rest of FY2026 are now expected to be completed in FY2027, it said in a business update on Wednesday. The group is also currently undertaking valuations of its property portfolio, which it noted “may give rise to impairment losses”. Shares of CDL closed 1.2 per cent or S$0.09 lower at S$7.12 on Wednesday, before the update.

Sats : The air cargo handler and airline caterer posted a 2.8 per cent rise in net profit to S$81.1 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, from S$78.9 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to higher cargo and meal volumes and lower tax expenses, even as the Middle East conflict raised input costs and disrupted operations, it said on Wednesday. Earnings per share stood at S$0.054 for the quarter, up from S$0.053 the year before. Revenue for the quarter rose 9 per cent to S$1.71 billion, from S$1.57 billion. Shares of Sats closed 2.6 per cent or S$0.10 higher at S$4 on Wednesday, before the news.

AEM : The semiconductor equipment maker’s net profit surged more than 18-fold to S$73.4 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 57.2 per cent to S$452.1 million on stronger demand for semiconductor testing solutions. AEM raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to S$680 million to S$705 million, from S$630 million to S$680 million, and its earnings per share guidance to S$0.30 to S$0.33, from S$0.245 to S$0.275. Shares of AEM closed 3.1 per cent or S$0.21 higher at S$7.05 on Wednesday.

StarHub : The telco reported a 26.3 per cent dip in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to S$72.1 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$97.8 million the prior year. Revenue rose to S$486.8 million, up 4.5 per cent from S$464.8 million previously. The telco said that despite rising revenue, Ebitda continued to decline because of lower gross profit, higher operating expenditure and lower income from other avenues. Shares of StarHub ended flat at S$1.04 on Wednesday.

NTT DC Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : The Reit on Wednesday posted a distribution per unit of US$0.0432 for the first half of FY2026/27, 10 per cent above its initial public offering projection, as net property income exceeded forecasts and net finance costs came in lower than expected. For the six months ended Sep 30, distributable income stood at US$45 million, against the projected US$40.9 million. Net property income was 4.9 per cent above projection at US$55.8 million, while gross revenue came in 2 per cent higher at US$119.8 million. Units of NTT DC Reit fell 2.2 per cent or US$0.02 to close at US$0.90 on Wednesday, before the news.

SBS Transit : The public transport operator posted a 35.5 per cent rise in net profit to S$19.6 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$14.5 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to a S$13 million write-back of prior years’ Fuel Equalisation Fund provisions, which was included in the operating profit. Operating profit for the quarter rose 37.7 per cent to S$22.6 million, from S$16.4 million in the year-ago period. Revenue fell 1.1 per cent to S$382.1 million from a year earlier due to a lower bus service fee from the loss of the Tampines package, as well as lower rail grants and ridership. Shares of SBS Transit closed flat at S$3.56 on Wednesday.

Centurion : The accommodation provider reported a 35 per cent rise in revenue to S$280.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$208.3 million in the previous corresponding period. This was mainly due to the consolidation of Westlite Mandai and new operational beds in Singapore, as well as its Harum Megah portfolio in Malaysia and Epiisod Macquarie Park in Australia. Revenue for the third quarter ended Sep 30 rose 41 per cent to S$95.2 million, it said in a business update. Shares of Centurion fell 2.4 per cent or S$0.03 to close at S$1.21 on Wednesday.

data.title: âSense of moral betrayalâ: High-profile charity scandal threatens donor trust in Thailand
data.description:
[BANGKOK] A scandal involving a charity run by a former beauty queen has left the Thai authorities scrambling to conduct a check on charities and foundations across the country.

Panadda “Boom” Wongphudee, 50, who won Miss Thailand in 2000, was arrested on Nov 6, along with her husband Atip Anantawan, 53, on charges including public fraud and money laundering.

About 527 million baht (US$15.5 million) out of 815 million baht donated to Ongkorn Thamdee, known in English as the Do Good Foundation, was allegedly siphoned off for the couple’s personal use to pay credit card bills, buy luxury goods and build a pool villa in Phuket.

Observers say the case shows that Thailand’s regulations governing charitable organisations are often outdated and not enforced consistently, highlighting the need for greater transparency.

“These cases keep coming back, and each time the money is larger and the method is the same: donations go into a personal account that nobody checks,” said Boonwara Sumano, a research fellow at the Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI).

According to Thailand’s 1944 Fund Raising Control Act, one requirement is that fund raising can be done only after applying for a permit. Another requires the fund-raiser to announce to the public, from time to time, the total money and property received and paid out.

But following investigations of the Do Good Foundation, the authorities revealed on Nov 4 that it had failed to submit income and expenditure statements or annual balance sheets since its registration in 2022.

“This foundation ran large campaigns through social media, including for flood relief, and the system showed no record of it ever applying for a permit. The authorities only noticed after the scandal broke,” Boonwara said.

She added that different government departments are responsible for checking on different requirements of an organisation, resulting in a situation where “each agency assumes another one is watching”.  

The latest scandal comes after the September arrest of a 66-year-old abbot accused of embezzling 100 million baht from Wat Phutthaisawan, a historic royal monastery in Ayutthaya, about 80 km north of Bangkok.

Local media reported that Thailand has about 50,000 temples and more than 30,000 foundations, associations and other non-profit organisations. 

Strong beliefs in merit, karma

Despite the probe into the Do Good Foundation, analysts said it is unfair to paint the entire philanthropy industry with one brush. Many non-governmental charity foundations help complement official measures.

Purawich Watanasukh, a political science lecturer at Thammasat University, said that during a crisis when the government response is slow or inadequate, charities help provide immediate, urgent assistance.

Donations are a huge part of the culture in Thailand, a Buddhist nation, given people’s strong beliefs in merit and good karma, he observed.

“Allegations involving charitable donations can provoke a particularly strong sense of moral betrayal,” he said, especially when donors feel their generosity and beliefs have been exploited.

During the flooding in several provinces in September and October, Do Good Foundation’s Panadda was seen wading through waist-high water wearing a life jacket, delivering aid to affected residents.

It was no surprise that Panadda, a former television presenter, singer and actress, elicited substantial amounts of donations, but this added another dimension to the breach of trust.

“Many have regarded her as a symbol of generosity and trustworthiness. Allegations that call this image into question can therefore generate a particularly profound sense of betrayal,” Purawich said. 

Although Panadda has made a public apology, at least 10 donors have filed complaints against her foundation, alleging the misuse of funds intended for flood victims, local media reported.

“The broader lesson is that personal reputation cannot provide sufficient assurance of organisational integrity,” Purawich said.

“Public trust needs clear rules, financial disclosure, independent scrutiny and meaningful accountability.”

Charity sector reforms needed

On Nov 7, a spokesperson for Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said a nationwide inspection of all foundations is meant to “prevent the establishment of front foundations or the use of donations for personal gain”.

“Furthermore, the operation of foundations must adhere to the principles of transparency, accountability and alignment with their registered objectives, especially the management of donations and foundation assets,” the spokesperson added.

But Dhiyathad Prateeppornnarong, a lecturer at the Graduate School of Public Administration at the National Institute of Development Administration, remains sceptical that any real change will occur, based on past examples such as promises of tighter gun control, which fell into a black hole.

“I hope that some big change will happen, but my suspicion is it may not. Because in Thailand, when the government is dealing with issues of high sensitivity like this, sometimes they like to wait and see whether or not the storm will subside,” he said.

Dhiyathad believes this case will not be the last, as it reflects a deeper problem in Thailand where charitable organisations are not held to the same level of scrutiny and accountability as corporations.

He suggested that the authorities conduct thorough screenings of those who apply to set up charities.

“The problem is that officials just check the formal documentation when anyone wants to set up a foundation,” he said.

“But it lacks the practical mechanism to check whether or not the person is really capable of managing it in accordance with the corporate governance principles and the benefits that the public will receive from running that foundation,” he added.

Thammasat University’s Purawich said that “the broader challenge is to ensure organisations receiving public donations can demonstrate how they manage and use those funds”.

TDRI’s Boonwara suggested reforms such as mandating that public donations go directly into accounts under a foundation’s name, safeguarded by several authorised signatories.

She also proposed requiring banks to flag personal accounts that receive large sums of donor transfers and requiring all donations made through public appeals to be made electronically.

“The public’s goodwill is a social asset worth protecting, and blind trust is not a substitute for a system. We should be able to give with faith and still ask for receipts.” THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: Singtel, ST Engg, Genting, First Resources, Golden Agri, CDG, Bumitama, Food Empire
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 13):

Singtel : The telecommunications giant on Friday posted a 55 per cent decline in net profit to S$1.54 billion for the first half-year ended September, from S$3.4 billion in the year-ago period. This was mainly due to the absence of S$2.21 billion in net exceptional gains recorded a year earlier from the partial sale of its stake in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Excluding exceptional items, underlying net profit rose 10 per cent to S$1.49 billion, from S$1.35 billion a year earlier. The company declared a 10 per cent higher interim dividend of S$0.09 per share. Singtel closed S$0.01 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$4.15 on Thursday.

ST Engineering : The technology and engineering group posted a 9 per cent year-on-year increase in revenue to S$3.4 billion for the third quarter ended September, from S$3.1 billion a year earlier, it said on Friday. It also declared a third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share, up from S$0.04 a year earlier. Together with its first- and second-quarter dividends of S$0.04 and S$0.05 per share, respectively, this brings the total dividend for the first nine months to S$0.14 per share. ST Engineering closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$9.76 on Thursday.

Genting Singapore : The integrated resort operator posted a 42.2 per cent fall in net profit to S$54.7 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$94.6 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for the quarter fell 12.9 per cent to S$566.1 million, from S$649.8 million a year earlier. Gaming revenue at Resorts World Sentosa (RWS), the group’s Singapore integrated resort, dropped 21.7 per cent to S$315 million in Q3, from S$402.3 million in the year-ago period. Genting Singapore said that renewal works at RWS will constrain operating capacity through 2027. Genting Singapore closed Thursday at S$0.61, down S$0.005 or 0.8 per cent.

First Resources : The palm oil producer posted a 40.1 per cent rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from US$87.5 million a year ago. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palm plants, it said. Sales was up 24.9 per cent to US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million a year ago. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. Shares of First Resources closed flat at S$2.79 on Thursday.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil company posted a net profit of US$162 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, a 32 per cent increase from US$123 million in the previous quarter. The rise in net profit was due primarily to higher plantation output and investment income received in Q3 2026, the company said. Revenue for Q3 was up 3 per cent at US$3.5 billion on a quarterly basis, supported by an appreciation in crude palm oil prices. Its shares ended Thursday 1.9 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.27.

ComfortDelGro (CDG) : The taxi operator posted a 20 per cent fall in net profit to S$141.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$176.4 million in the previous corresponding period. It said its taxi and private-hire business was hit by competition and cautious consumer spending. Revenue for the nine months rose 4.9 per cent to S$3.94 billion from S$3.75 billion the year before, supported by contracted public transport operations. The company is bidding for more public transport contracts, with opportunities available from 2026 to 2028 estimated at more than S$17 billion. CDG closed flat at S$1.29 on Thursday.

Bumitama : The palm oil producer reported a 2 per cent increase in its net profit to 614 billion rupiah (US$34 million) for the quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, compared with 603 billion rupiah from the corresponding period a year ago. For the nine months ended Sep 30, 2026, net profit rose 31 per cent to 2.4 trillion rupiah from a year ago. The company said its performance was supported by improvements in productivity in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. Shares of Bumitama closed flat at S$1.39 on Thursday.

Food Empire : The company posted an 11.7 per cent rise in revenue to a record US$476.5 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from US$426.7 million in the previous corresponding period. This was driven mainly by its core Russia and Central Asia segments. For its third quarter ended Sep 30, revenue rose 5.8 per cent to US$161.4 million, from US$152.6 million a year earlier. This was driven by growth across its core segments and partly offset by a 5.2 per cent decline in Europe. Food Empire closed flat at S$1.79 on Thursday.

data.title: Nvidia crisis: âEmperorâ Huangâs downfall may blow US-China AI race wide open
data.description:
THE memes, influencer gags and Reddit rabbit holes surrounding Jensen Huang’s infidelity have made for irresistible entertainment.

But surely, the most consequential question arising from this saga is what it means for the frontier artificial intelligence race between the US and China.

The memes, influencer gags and Reddit rabbit holes surrounding Jensen Huang’s infidelity have made for irresistible entertainment.

But surely, the most consequential question arising from this saga is what it means for the frontier artificial intelligence race between the US and China.

Huang is no ordinary tech CEO. He is, in the words of his biographer Stephen Witt, the “emperor of AI”. The entire AI ecosystem, whether in the US or China, depends heavily on Nvidia, which dominates the market for graphics processing units that power AI development.

The multitrillion-dollar chipmaker is also effectively the central bank of AI, helping to finance the infrastructure expansion of companies that, in turn, buy its chips.

It is increasingly venturing into AI model development itself. Through all of that, Nvidia has fused its public identity, success and reputation with those of its founder.

In a reality where “Nvidia is Jensen, and Jensen is Nvidia”, what happens to the West’s lead over China now that he has resigned? Right now, that lead is about a year, going by US President Donald Trump’s estimate in his Nov 8 interview with 60 Minutes.

There are several strands to this story, each worth weighing.

The cost of Nvidia chaos

The first aligns with most people’s instincts: Nvidia is certain to be destabilised by Huang’s departure and the transition to new leadership.

That would send shockwaves across the US AI industry and, by extension, the entire Western tech stack, which is essentially American.

The logic is straightforward. A change of the guard, on top of a grilling by US lawmakers in upcoming committee hearings and ongoing Federal Bureau of Investigation probes, will consume immense bandwidth within the company.

A successor will also have to contend with a company built around one man. Huang has wielded concentrated power, with every major decision running through him.

The seating arrangement at Nvidia’s California headquarters reportedly reflected this: His top lieutenants sat in a stadium-style arc facing his enormous oval desk.

This risk of institutional paralysis has been flagged by experts such as Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics and security programme at the Center for a New American Security in Washington.

Speaking to news portal The Verge, she raised the possibility that internal distractions could hurt Nvidia’s ability to execute.

Slower decisions, delayed product roll-outs or hiccups in the allocation of scarce chips could hit major US players such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Both are trying to wean themselves off Nvidia hardware, but those efforts are still in the early stages.

In the race to build ever more powerful AI, time is precious. Even modest delays for American companies could help Chinese rivals catch up.

They do have ground to make up. China’s mass buying of Nvidia chips, including older generations that Huang lobbied the White House to allow, shows how far Beijing lags in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

That is partly because the West’s technological moat lies in chipmaking equipment subject to US-led export controls.

Nvidia-designed processors are made using highly specialised extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines produced solely by Dutch firm ASML.

China is said to be within two to five years of high-volume manufacturing of less capable deep ultraviolet machines, while EUV technology remains a distant prospect.

All of that is the extreme scenario: Nvidia falls into chaos and China capitalises, using the opening to make further inroads into frontier AI development.

The case for resilience

Yet some pundits, including those who spoke to this columnist, take a diametrically opposed view. They argue that even with the outsized Huang factor, Nvidia and its wider ecosystem have enough built-in resilience to weather the storm, leaving the Western AI lead intact.

Paul Mah, a Singapore-based senior adviser specialising in South-east Asian data centres at consultancy Flint Global, said the company’s fundamentals remained unshaken. He pointed to its “global and diversified ecosystem, its existing technological moat, its technical prowess and its end-to-end partnerships”.

Tech commentator Mehran Gul agreed that Nvidia remained resilient as an institution in the near term. “Turmoil at the top” would not affect already-designed chips shipping over the next two years or pre-booked manufacturing capacity at Taiwanese foundry TSMC.

Nor would it affect Nvidia’s software moat, notably CUDA, the proprietary platform that allows developers to program its graphics chips for the heavy computing that underpins AI applications.

Gul, author of the book The New Geography Of Innovation, added that any longer-term impact from Huang’s departure would be financial and political rather than technological, tied to Nvidia’s balance sheet, its share price and Huang’s role as chief dealmaker and diplomat.

In his telling, this would not move the needle much for China. The West’s AI lead, he noted, rests on a layered, globally distributed system: Dutch lithography from ASML, Taiwanese fabrication, South Korean high-bandwidth memory chips and American design and capital.

A third scenario is that some pain for Nvidia might actually help secure the West’s AI lead in the long run.

If the crisis blunts the company’s near-monopoly, competitors could get more than a foot in the door, turning a single-company bottleneck into a healthier oligopoly of AI processor makers.

Mah cited Google’s roll-out of a broad array of AI chips, including the latest versions of its tensor processing units – custom-made semiconductors used to develop and run AI software.

Once reserved for the tech giant’s own use, these are now available to outside customers, with Apple, Meta, Oracle, Anthropic and OpenAI either already buying or planning to sign on.

Smaller rivals such as Nevada-based startup Positron could also gain ground.

It drew attention in 2026 after raising US$875 million (S$1.1 billion) at a valuation of US$5 billion, buoyed by investor appetite for its Asimov AI processor. Still, the circular nature of AI financing, with Nvidia bankrolling a sizeable part of the infrastructure expansion that drives demand for its chips, remains a wild card.

Another critical variable is what happens next with export controls.

Once the Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, they are widely expected to come out guns blazing, accusing the Trump administration of paying lip service to restrictions and pushing for far tighter enforcement. Chuck Schumer, the putative Senate majority leader, has already intimated as much.

From there, things could go two ways.

On the one hand, China could be seriously squeezed. Beijing has gone out of its way to amass lower-end Nvidia chips and, if the espionage allegations linked to the Huang affair are to be believed, has left no stone unturned to acquire them.

A fierce US clampdown could even choke off Chinese firms’ remote access to computing power through South-east Asian data centres.

Taiwan-born Huang has long been the most prominent advocate of continued engagement with China rather than ever tighter restrictions. Self-serving, perhaps, but his publicly stated case was that keeping Chinese developers dependent on American technology served US interests better than shutting them out.

On the other hand, given how assiduously Beijing has pursued technological self-reliance, a harder line from Washington may simply accelerate that push. As Gul put it: “If the controversy hardens Washington’s stance on chip exports, it reinforces Beijing’s push for self-sufficiency, which was already well under way.”

Turning point for AI

There is little doubt that this is a turning point for the AI era, perhaps the most consequential jolt since ChatGPT’s debut in late 2022.

Beyond the gyrations in Nvidia’s share price and the tabloid neck-craning over Huang’s human frailties and hubris, these competing scenarios demand scrutiny by governments in Asia and beyond as they chart their own digital futures.

Should the episode derail AI momentum, it could upend well-laid national plans across the region, where governments have rolled out the welcome mat for multibillion-dollar data centres.

More broadly, the crisis is a timely stress test of technological dependencies. For the Western AI stack, a supply chain stretching from California to Tainan, the question is whether it is truly resilient enough to be trusted as global infrastructure.

If it can come undone over one man – who, despite his immense achievements, largely brought about his own downfall – then countries that have rushed to tether themselves to American AI without considering the Chinese alternative have some hard thinking to do.

For China, meanwhile, the question is whether the rival it has been stalking in AI is going through a mere blip or has genuine vulnerabilities.

If turmoil at Nvidia cascades into a wider crisis across the West’s AI world, disrupting investment, innovation and roll-out, Beijing could gain an opening that did not exist even a month ago. Whether it has the wherewithal and the will to pounce is another matter. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: The longevity boom is measuring the wrong thing
data.description:
A FEW years ago a man in his late 60s came to see me – not as a patient, since I am a researcher and not a physician, but because he had heard I studied ageing and he wanted to show me his numbers.

He had the grip strength of a man 20 years younger, a resting heart rate an athlete would envy, and a report declaring his body a decade younger than his chronological age.

He laid the printouts on my desk with great care. Then he mentioned, almost in passing, that he no longer knew what he was keeping all this health for: His wife had died. His children lived abroad. He woke each morning, did his exercises, took his supplements, and waited for a day that did not especially need him.

I have spent two decades measuring ageing – building and validating the kinds of indices that tell how well or badly a person is growing old.

I think about that man often because he had won – comprehensively – the game the entire longevity industry is now urging everyone to play.

But he was among the most desolate people I had met.

We are now living through an extraordinary enthusiasm for measuring how fast we age. For a few hundred dollars, a mail-order kit will read the chemical tags on your DNA and assign ages to your heart, lungs and brain. Devotees feed the results to chatbots that prescribe the next peptide, the next panel, the next scan.

The global longevity market is a multi-billion-dollar industry, growing on a simple, seductive promise: If we can measure ageing precisely enough, we can manage it – and doing so will make a long life good.

Singapore has caught the “biohacking” fever with particular intensity. The affluent now pay five-figure sums for longevity memberships and personalised “transformation” plans. Clinics here offer the full menu: DNA-based biological-age tests, bone-density scans, AI-read diagnostics.

Tellingly, a growing share of the clientele are not the old but optimisers in their 30s, tracking their visceral fat and cortisol.

At every price point, the same promise is presented: Measure the body precisely enough, and you can manage its decline.

There is a deeper irony here, one that a nation counting the cost of ageing cannot miss. The people fuelling this boom – the affluent, the already-fit, the 30-something optimisers – have the least left to gain, chasing the last few per cent near the ceiling of health.

The largest gains in healthy years and the real savings from illnesses prevented lie at the other end of the social gradient – among the frail and financially vulnerable, where a modest intervention still goes a long way.

The market sends its resources precisely where they yield the least.

The questions that matter

Let me say plainly what is true, because I build these instruments and believe in them. Chronological age is a blunt tool; people of the same age differ enormously in health and resilience, and capturing that difference biologically is a genuine scientific prize.

But the current enthusiasm has outrun the science. An algorithm trained to predict the number of birthdays you have had does not thereby reveal which processes are driving your decline. A biological-age score, as a major 2026 synthesis underscores, predicts without explaining.

The honest frontier is harder and far more interesting than a number on an app.

For the next 10 years, the real question is not whether we can measure ageing, or even nudge it. It is whether we can work out which biological processes are actually driving ageing in a particular person, at a specific point in their life – and whether changing those processes would make a real difference to how healthy and able they stay.

That is a frontier worth every dollar we can give it. But suppose we win it. Suppose that within a generation we can read a person’s ageing with precision and slow it where it matters. It would still be biology.

It can keep a body able, yet it cannot tell that body what the ability is for, or what the person is worth on the day the ability finally goes.

The fitter we make the body, the more nakedly it hands us back the questions biology was never built to answer.

The evidence from my field is consistent. What makes a long life bearable is not a low biological age. It is purpose, belonging, and the sense that one’s life still matters to someone.

None of that is read by a clock or sold for a fee, and the measurement culture can actively corrode it.

A recent report in The New York Times followed two sisters who tested their biological ages and found the kit became a “ledger” of their lives, delivering not clarity, but feelings they could not quantify.

A poorer score and sad-face icons on the health report tipped the disciplined, health-conscious sister into a “private vortex of grief”, wondering where her regime had gone awry.

The deepest human goods run on the opposite logic to the ledger: They are conferred, not achieved; granted before anything is accomplished. A grandchild does not love you more for a younger liver.

Singapore, which will soon count one in four citizens over 65, has built some of the most advanced ageing infrastructure in the world.

Yet the research suggests that the societies that age best are not the ones with the best biomarkers. They are the ones that keep their old people needed, connected and seen.

The hardest problem of a long life is not metabolic. It is whether, at 90, there is still anyone for whom your being alive makes a difference.

We have spent a fortune learning to measure how fast we age. We have spent almost nothing on the only questions that finally decide whether a long life is a gift or a sentence: what the added years are for, and what a person is worth when the measuring stops.

That is the frontier that matters now. It will not yield to a blood test – and it is the one we are leaving unfunded.

The writer is a gerontologist at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, where he researches and teaches healthy ageing, frailty and dementia. He is editing a forthcoming volume, Ageing Well Together: Faith, Science and Community for an Asian Ageing Society.

data.title: Most Microsoft services in Sâpore restored after outage that lasted more than 24 hours
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Most e-mail services here have been restored on Nov 14, a day after a Microsoft outage that affected hundreds of thousands of users globally.

Various statutory boards and government agencies including the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore, Singapore Land Authority, Singhealth and the Singapore Police Force noted in separate Facebook posts late on Nov 13 and on the morning of Nov 14 that their e-mail services are up and running.

Banks such as DBS, UOB and Maybank have also updated on their respective Facebook pages that their e-mail services have been restored.

Reports of issues with Microsoft Outlook peaked at 1,135 at about 9.30 am in Singapore on Nov 13, gradually falling to 347 at about 8.45 pm on the same day.

In a media reply on Nov 13, the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) confirmed that some government systems were hit by the disruption, adding that it was working with Microsoft to restore the affected services.

The private and education sectors were also affected by the outage, with banks here reporting e-mail disruptions, though core banking operations were unaffected.

The e-mail services for Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) were also affected by the disruption.

The outage, reports of which started climbing around 5.25 pm GMT on Nov 12 (1.25 am on Nov 13, Singapore time) according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services in 2026, Reuters reported.

Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online – its cloud-based e-mail and scheduling hub – leaving unconnected applications operational.

Reuters reported that Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

Microsoft said in an update posted on X at 12.40 am on Nov 14 that it saw “broad recovery and stability” across its services.

It clarified that the issue was not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the post added.

Microsoft also said that it will provide a full post-incident report once its review is complete.

The Straits Times has contacted GovTech for more information. THE STRAITS TIMES
